title: The wounded healer
hookLine: people who have suffered sometimes become healers, an old idea found in myths and in modern care alike

cards: In Greek myth there's a centaur named Chiron, half man, half horse, who lives in a cave on a mountain and teaches young heroes. He knows herbs, music and medicine.

In some tellings he teaches healing to Asclepius, who becomes the god of medicine. And Chiron carries a wound of his own: an arrow, poisoned, that struck him by accident. He is immortal, so he cannot die of it.
And it will not heal. That strange picture has followed people a long way, into churches and clinics. It has a name.

teach.b: First, the myth. Chiron's wound doesn't stop his work. In the story, it sits right beside it.

Much later, the psychiatrist Carl Jung wrote of the wounded physician: the idea that a healer's own hurt can be part of what lets them understand a patient's. Writers after him tied that phrase to Chiron.
Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, puts the same idea in Christian terms.
He calls God the one "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

Comfort received becomes comfort passed on. The Catholic priest Henri Nouwen wrote a whole book called The Wounded Healer, about how a minister's own loneliness and pain can become a place where others find welcome.
Third, the room down the hall.

teach.h: SOMEONE WHO HAS BEEN THROUGH IT.
teach.b: Some recovery groups are built on it: a person who has been through it, sitting with a person going through it.

Some hospitals and clinics bring in peer supporters, people with lived experience of an illness, to sit beside those newly facing it. Nobody has to explain what the first night feels like. Fourth, a caution.
Nobody owes their wound to anyone, and some wounds are still too open to lend out.

teach.h: FROM A SCAR, NOT A FRESH CUT.
teach.b: One way to put it: help from a scar, not from a fresh cut.
On some days, you are the one who needs the soup. On others, what you came through may be what someone else needs to hear.

how: Some recovery groups and peer support programs pair people who have come through an illness, addiction or loss with those newly facing it, and some Christians read 2 Corinthians 1:4 as a call to pass on the comfort they have received.

games.q: a friend has just been told what you were told a few years ago. your own story still aches a little. what do you do?
o: tell them your whole story so they know what's coming.
offer the one thing that helped you, and listen.
stay away; it isn't your business.
games.why: the wounded healer offers from a scar: one thing that helped, then presence. Paul's word is comfort, passed on, not a lecture.

practice: Let one hard thing you've come through come to mind, one that has begun to heal, not one still raw, and ask quietly what you learned there that someone else might need: a phone number, a sentence that helped, something nobody told you at the start.
Then hold in mind one person near the beginning of something like it, and what you might offer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Chiron, the wounded centaur of Greek myth whose own hurt never closes, and who still teaches healing to others. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the wound helps. What you came through may light the way for someone just starting out. See you tomorrow.
